overview:
Zambia is a landlocked country in south-central Africa, shaped a little like a butterfly and about the size of Texas. It borders eight countries, one of the highest totals on the continent, and shares Victoria Falls with Zimbabwe on the Zambezi River, the river that gives the country its name. Lusaka, the capital, stands on a high plateau in the south-center.

About 20 million people live in Zambia, in more than 70 ethnic groups. English is the official language, used in schools and government, while Bemba, Nyanja, Tonga and Lozi are the main languages spoken at home. Zambia is a republic. Copper has shaped the country for a century: the Copperbelt in the north is one of the world's major mining regions, and the metal still earns most of Zambia's export income. Farming, especially maize, feeds most families, and vast national parks draw visitors who explore them on foot.
landAndNature: Zambia is mostly high savanna plateau, between roughly 1,000 and 1,400 meters up, which takes the edge off the tropical heat. The Zambezi crosses the west and south and drops 108 meters over Victoria Falls in a curtain more than 1.7 kilometers wide; the spray rises hundreds of meters, and the local name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means the smoke that thunders. Lake Kariba, formed by damming the Zambezi, is one of the largest reservoirs on Earth. The Bangweulu swamps hold shoebill storks and the water-loving black lechwe antelope. South Luangwa National Park is known for leopards, elephants and guided walking safaris.
peopleAndCulture: Nshima, a thick maize porridge, is eaten by hand with relish dishes of greens, beans, fish or chicken at nearly every meal. Kapenta, tiny dried fish netted from Lake Tanganyika and Lake Kariba, is a common source of protein. Ceremonies mark the year across the regions, and the most spectacular is the Kuomboka, when the Lozi king travels by decorated barge from the flooding Zambezi plain to higher ground, escorted by drummers and dozens of paddlers. Soccer is the national sport, and Zambia's women's team has played at the Olympics and the World Cup. Kalindula music and rumba play in buses and markets.
history: People have lived here a very long time; the Broken Hill skull, found at Kabwe in 1921, belonged to an early human species and is roughly 300,000 years old. Bantu-speaking farmers and ironworkers settled the plateau, and kingdoms such as the Lozi and the Bemba took shape. In the late 1800s the British South Africa Company, led by Cecil Rhodes, claimed the territory, which became the colony of Northern Rhodesia, and copper mining boomed from the 1920s. Independence came on October 24, 1964, under Kenneth Kaunda, who governed for 27 years. Zambia sheltered liberation movements from neighboring countries, returned to multiparty elections in 1991, and has changed governments peacefully since.
funFacts: Victoria Falls is neither the tallest nor the widest waterfall, but together its height and width make the largest sheet of falling water on Earth.
When the river is low, swimmers sit in the Devil's Pool, a rock basin right at the lip of Victoria Falls.
Zambia borders eight countries, one of the highest numbers anywhere in Africa.
The Kuomboka ceremony moves the Lozi king by decorated barge whenever the Zambezi floods his palace grounds.
The shoebill of Zambia's Bangweulu swamps stands over a meter tall and has a bill shaped like a wooden clog.
